title: CELL: Fairness-aware Graph Adaptation Without Target Labels
one_liner: Predict fairly on a new graph by separating what matters for the task from what only reflects demographic groups, without needing the sensitive attributes of the new graph.
lead: Graphs (networks of connected items) encode relationships in real data — social networks, citation systems, disease spread. When you train a model on one graph to predict on another, the model often learns to use demographic features like race or gender unfairly, hurting certain groups. This paper fixes that by decomposing what the model learns into two pieces: features that predict the task honestly, and features that leak demographic information. By keeping only the honest piece and guessing the demographic attributes from the unlabeled target graph, the method works fairly even when you don't have target-graph sensitive attributes.

paras: You have a labeled training graph — say, a social network with nodes (people) and edges (friendships) — and a task like detecting who has a job. You train a model on it. Then you need to predict on a new unlabeled graph (a different social network). The naive approach: use the same model directly. This often fails not just because the graphs differ, but because the model has learned to use sensitive attributes (race, gender, age) as shortcuts to predict jobs. If the model learned 'women are less likely to have jobs' from the training data, it will unfairly penalize women in the new graph.

Standard fairness methods ask: what if we had the sensitive attributes (age, race, etc.) in the target graph too? Then we could force the model to ignore them there. But in reality, you usually cannot get that data — it is private, restricted, or simply not collected.

callout.html: Make a model that predicts fairly on a new unlabeled graph, even though you do not know the sensitive attributes there.

panels.title: 1. Training graph has bias
panels.caption: Model learns: high job rate means high scores, but also uses gender shortcut.

panels.title: 2. Naive transfer: bias carries over
panels.caption: Moving to target graph with same weights: gender bias now predicts falsely.

panels.title: 3. CELL splits the signal
panels.caption: One encoder finds honest task features; another extracts demographic shortcuts.

panels.title: 4. Block the bias path
panels.caption: Keep fair path, mute bias path on target: unfair shortcuts are silenced.

panels.title: 5. Guess attributes to guide alignment
panels.caption: Predict what target demographic labels likely are; use their structure to help.

steps.text: Train two encoders on the source graph: one learns features tied to task success (job prediction), the other learns demographic shortcuts (gender bias).
Measure how much information about the demographic features leaks into the task features. Push them apart by minimizing this crosstalk.
On the new unlabeled graph, guess what the demographic attributes probably are by looking at structure and the fair features.
Use a bipartite bridge graph (connecting source and target nodes in a fairness-aware way) to teach the model how graphs differ without using unfair shortcuts.

steps.b: Predict with only the fair path
steps.text: On target data, use only the task features, not the demographic encoder. Predictions now ignore the bias learned from source.

paras: CELL changes which features the model uses to make predictions. Instead of one jumbled set of features (both fair and biased), it creates two separate paths: one for honest task signals, one for demographic bias. Then it blocks the bias path at test time, so fairness is guaranteed.

hidden.name: how much demographic information is in the task features
paras: The paper measures something invisible: how much information about sensitive attributes (like gender or race) is accidentally baked into the features that predict the main task. This is called conditional mutual information — a number measuring how much two things tell you about each other when you already know a third thing. In this case: how much do the task features predict gender, given that you already know the task label?

CELL estimates this by looking at how much the demographic encoder's outputs overlap with the task encoder's outputs. If the demographic encoder can easily guess someone's gender from the task features, the leakage is high. The method then minimizes this overlap by pushing the two encoders to extract completely different things.

heat.caption: Darker task features mean more demographic signal leakage. CELL pushes leakage to zero (all light).

reads.html: The leakage is the degree to which knowing someone's task features tells you their demographic group.
Conditional mutual information between sensitive attribute and task features given task label, minimized during training.

mechanism.h2: Why separation and pseudo-labeling work together
paras: The core idea: if you force two encoders to extract completely different information (one for the task, one for demographics), the model stops using demographic shortcuts for the main prediction. The task encoder has no choice but to find real patterns.

But the target graph is unlabeled, so how do you know if the split is working there? CELL uses pseudo-labels — educated guesses about what the target demographic attributes probably are, inferred from the structure of the target graph and the fair features. These guesses give the demographic encoder something to latch onto, anchoring the separation even with no ground truth. The bipartite bridge graph (links between source and target nodes chosen fairly) provides additional structural hints about how graphs differ, steering alignment without bias.
Result: the task features generalize to the target because they encode real task patterns, not dataset shortcuts. The demographic path is silenced at test time, removing unfair predictions.

stages.s: source graph with labels + target graph without labels
train sensitive and causal encoders on source; minimize their crosstalk
guess target demographics from structure; mark high-confidence nodes
build fairness-aware bridge connecting source and target
use only task encoder on target, ignore demographic encoder

math.words: minimize task loss plus weighted crosstalk between task and demographic encoders, plus alignment loss with the bridge graph
math.equation: L_total = L_task + lambda_d * I(Z_s; Z_t | Y) + lambda_align * L_bridge
symbols: task prediction error on source graph
how much demographic features Z_s overlap with task features Z_t, knowing the label Y (the leakage)
weight controlling how hard to enforce separation
alignment loss from the fairness-aware bridge graph

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say task encoder learns: person-A has features (job=0.8, gender-leakage=0.3). Demographic encoder independently learns: person-A is female (0.9). Crosstalk I(Z_s; Z_t) is high because task features hint at gender.
CELL adds penalty: lambda_d * 0.3 * 0.9 = 0.15 to loss, pushing them apart.
After training, task features are (job=0.8, gender-leakage=0.01). Now demographic encoder cannot guess gender from task features. Crosstalk penalty shrinks to 0.01 * 0.9 = 0.009.
At test time on target: predict using only (job=0.8, irrelevant-noise=0.01), ignore the demographic encoder. Fairness is intact because no gender signal remains in the task path.

math.note: The equation enforces that task and demographic encoders extract unrelated information. Separating them works because a demographic encoder with no task information is forced to find demographic shortcuts instead of task patterns, so the task encoder must use real task signals. The bridge helps both paths generalize without bias by teaching alignment through fair node pairs.

charts.title: Naive transfer (all features)
charts.note: All features transferred, including demographic shortcuts; accuracy drops on target and fairness is poor.

charts.title: CELL (separated & aligned)
charts.note: Fair features generalize better because they encode real task patterns, not dataset shortcuts tied to the source graph's demographics. Demographic shortcuts are blocked at test time because the demographic encoder is never used. Both accuracy and fairness improve on target because the model now relies only on honest signals.

items.html: If the guessed target demographic attributes are inaccurate, the demographic encoder trains on false data, and separation may leak unfair features into the task path. Confidence thresholding helps by ignoring low-confidence pseudo-labels, but does not fully fix this because some structure may always mislead the guessing algorithm.
If the fairness-aware bipartite graph connects dissimilar source and target nodes, it teaches the model wrong alignment, reducing generalization.

items.b: Task and demographics are truly entangled.
items.html: In real data, the task and a sensitive attribute may have genuine overlap (e.g., a job role may legitimately correlate with education level). Forcing complete separation can hurt accuracy.

Pseudo-labels are high-confidence — for example, if the target graph has structural homophily (friends tend to have the same gender), the method can group similar nodes reliably. The bridge is learned jointly with encoders so it adapts as the encoders separate task and demographic signals. The method is tuned to allow some task-relevant correlation (e.g., if education truly predicts the job) while blocking pure demographic shortcuts (e.g., gender alone predicting the job), because the loss function penalizes only the crosstalk between demographic and task encoders: if a feature helps both the task and accidentally encodes demographics, the penalty is small, but if it helps only demographics, the penalty is large.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small citation graph (papers and authors, with edges for authorship). Train CELL on one conference as the source (with known author genders) to predict whether a paper will be cited frequently. Test on papers from a different time period or venue (the target), without gender labels. Show that: (1) naive transfer predicts citation unfairly (predicts lower citations for papers by women even at the same quality); (2) CELL predicts citations more fairly (gender gap shrinks), while keeping accuracy high.
demo.closing: The demo must make it clear that CELL sacrifices little accuracy to achieve fairness, and that the gap between groups is small even though the target graph has no gender labels.
